reading.body:
Connecticut has 8 MW of publicly disclosed data center IT load, and CyrusOne's Norwalk campus holds half of it at 4 MW.

That total comes from only two of the five mapped data center facilities in the state. The other three publish no power specification, so the visible megawatts are a floor rather than a census. For AI this matters because compute is bounded by delivered power, and a facility map without megawatts cannot tell you where training capacity could actually sit. Norwalk ranks first in Connecticut on published capacity by default, which is a statement about disclosure as much as about the building.

The facility itself pairs 4 MW of IT load with 168,000 square feet of technical space. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 4 MW is roughly 100 racks. Its SSAE 16 Type II certification covers audited controls over physical and logical access, which fits regulated and security-sensitive tenants rather than describing compute capability. Nothing in the published figures indicates a power density or a hall size aimed at large training clusters.

What the data does not cover is decisive here. There is no announced expansion, no utility or interconnection detail, no address, and no quantified proximity to the Northeast corridor. The suitability score of 49 rests on published IT capacity and operator type alone, with announced expansion listed as missing. So the record describes a certified colocation site of modest published size, and cannot say whether it is a toehold for something larger.
